title: Design File Sync (Dropbox-like)
subtitle: Edit one spot in a 100 MiB file and watch only 4 MB travel, then see how your other laptop learns about it.
learn: How files are split into content-hashed blocks, and why identical blocks are stored once
Why file metadata and file bytes live in two different stores
How a device finds out what changed, using a cursor instead of trusting notifications
How delta sync moves only changed blocks in both directions
How to detect a conflict with base versions and resolve it without losing data

steps.title: One small edit, one big file
steps.body: You fix a typo in a 100 MiB slide deck on Laptop A. Laptop B should show the fix within seconds. The naive plan is to upload all 100 MiB and make B download all 100 MiB. Multiply that by millions of users saving files all day and the bandwidth bill is absurd. We want to move only what changed.
steps.idea: Sync is a bandwidth problem first: send the change, not the file.
steps.caption: A 100 MiB file changed on Laptop A.

steps.title: Cut the file into blocks
steps.body: The sync client splits the file into fixed 4 MiB blocks, so 100 MiB becomes about 25 blocks. It computes a SHA-256 hash of each block; the hash is the block's name, because identical bytes always give the same hash. The file is now just an ordered list of 25 hashes. This all happens locally, before any network call. Assume the app edits in place and keeps the length, as with a database file, disk image or raw media; zipped formats like .pptx can shift bytes, which the trade-off step covers.
steps.idea: A file becomes an ordered list of content hashes, and a block's name is its content.
steps.caption: Laptop A hashes 25 blocks locally.

steps.title: Ask which blocks are missing
steps.body: Laptop A sends the 25 hashes to the Sync API. The API checks the metadata database to see which hashes already exist in the block store. Only one hash is unknown, because the edit changed just one block; the other 24 are unchanged from the previous version. The same check also dedups across files and users: a block the system already holds is never uploaded again.
steps.idea: Because blocks are named by content, the server can say exactly which ones it still needs.
steps.caption: Server replies: need 1 of 25 blocks.

steps.title: Upload only the changed block
steps.body: Laptop A uploads the single 4 MiB block straight to the block store, usually with a short-lived signed URL the API handed out, so file bytes never pass through the API servers. Blocks are immutable: written once under their hash, never modified. That makes retries safe, since re-uploading the same block just writes identical bytes. The store (or a verifier) recomputes the SHA-256 of what arrives and rejects a mismatch, so a block's name can be trusted.
steps.idea: Immutable, content-addressed blocks make uploads idempotent (doing it twice has the same effect as once) and cacheable.
steps.caption: One 4 MiB block reaches the block store.

steps.title: Commit the new version
steps.body: Now the client tells the API: file /deck.pptx version 8 is this list of 25 hashes, built on top of version 7. The database applies it only if the head is still v7, appends an entry to the user's change log, and checks that every listed block exists, all in one transaction. Metadata is small, relational, and needs strong consistency; blocks are huge, dumb, and need cheap durable storage. Committing only after all blocks exist means no version ever points at a missing block.
steps.idea: Keep tiny, consistent metadata apart from huge, immutable bytes, and commit metadata last.
steps.caption: Metadata DB records version 8.

steps.title: Tell the other devices
steps.body: After the commit, the API publishes a tiny event to the notify service: something changed in this user's folder. Laptop B holds a long-lived connection (long poll or WebSocket) to it and receives a ping. The ping carries no file data and may be lost, delayed, or duplicated. It is only a nudge to go ask for changes.
steps.idea: Notifications are a cheap hint to wake a device up, not the source of truth.
steps.caption: A small ping reaches Laptop B.

steps.title: Laptop B pulls the delta
steps.body: Laptop B asks the API for changes since its cursor, a position number it saved after its last sync. The API answers that deck.pptx is now version 8 with a new hash list. B compares it to the list it already has, finds one hash it lacks, and downloads just that block, then reassembles the file locally. If the ping had been lost, B would still catch up on its next poll or reconnect, because the cursor makes the question safe to repeat.
steps.idea: A cursor turns sync into 'give me everything after N', which is repeatable and loss-tolerant.
steps.caption: B downloads one block, not 100 MiB.

steps.title: Both laptops edited offline
steps.body: Suppose B was offline and edited the same file from version 7, while A already committed version 8. When B reconnects and commits 'new version on top of 7', the API sees the current head is 8, not 7, and rejects it with a conflict. Last-writer-wins by timestamp would silently destroy one person's work, and device clocks are unreliable. Instead the server keeps v8 and B's edit is saved as a separate 'conflicted copy' for a human to merge.
steps.idea: Detect conflicts by comparing base version to head; resolve by keeping both rather than guessing.
steps.caption: Commit on stale base v7 is rejected.

steps.title: How big should a block be?
steps.body: Small blocks dedup and delta better but mean more hashes, more metadata rows, and more requests. Big blocks are cheap to track but resend more on each edit. About 4 MiB is a common middle ground. One weakness: fixed boundaries break when bytes are inserted near the start, because every later block shifts. Content-defined chunking, which picks cut points from the data itself, fixes that at the cost of more client CPU.
steps.idea: Block size trades metadata overhead against bytes resent; fixed cuts are simple, content-defined cuts survive insertions.
steps.caption: Block size balances metadata and bandwidth.

steps.title: Only the change travels
steps.body: The client chunks and hashes, the API dedups against known hashes, only missing blocks are uploaded to the block store, and a final atomic metadata commit publishes the version. A small notification wakes other devices, which pull changes after their cursor and fetch only new blocks. Conflicts are caught by base-version checks and kept as separate copies.
steps.idea: Hash blocks, store each once, commit metadata last, sync by cursor, and never silently overwrite.
steps.caption: A 100 MiB edit cost about 4 MB each way.

quiz.q: A 1 GiB file is stored as fixed 4 MiB blocks. You overwrite some bytes in the middle without changing the file length, touching one block. About how much must be uploaded?
options: The whole 1 GiB, since the file changed
About 1 MiB, the size of the edit
About 4 MiB, the one affected block
About 256 MiB, a quarter of the blocks
quiz.why: Only the block containing the edit gets a new hash. The other 255 blocks hash the same and are already stored, so one 4 MiB block moves.

quiz.q: Why does the client commit the new file version to the metadata database only after the blocks are uploaded?
options: So no committed version can reference a block that does not exist yet
Because the metadata database is faster than the block store
To make the upload bytes pass through the API
To avoid needing hashes at all
quiz.why: If metadata were committed first, another device could read a version whose blocks are missing. Blocks first, pointer last makes the commit the visible switch.

quiz.q: The notification service drops the ping for Laptop B during a brief outage. What keeps B from staying stale forever?
options: Laptop B stays stale until the user manually re-uploads the file
The Sync API pushes the whole file to B on every commit
B's clock detects the newer file timestamp
B asks for changes after its saved cursor when it reconnects or polls
quiz.why: Notifications are only hints. The cursor query returns every change after the last position B saw, so a missed ping delays sync but cannot lose a change.

quiz.q: Two devices edit the same file offline from version 7. Which handling best avoids losing work?
options: Keep whichever edit has the later device timestamp and drop the other
Reject the stale commit and keep both versions as a conflicted copy
Lock the file for every user at all times so edits never overlap
Merge the two files byte by byte automatically
quiz.why: Device clocks drift, so timestamp wins can destroy data, and generic byte merges corrupt binary formats. Detecting a stale base and keeping both copies is safe and simple.

cheatsheet.def: A fixed-size slice of a file (about 4 MiB here). The unit of upload, storage, and dedup.
Blocks are stored under the hash of their bytes, so equal content has one name and is stored once.
Skip storing or uploading a block already held. Caveat: cross-user dedup can reveal that someone has a file; dedup per account or require proof of possession.
Small, consistent records: paths, versions, ordered block-hash lists, sharing. Needs transactions and sharding by account.
Cheap, durable object storage for immutable blocks, with replication or erasure coding (splitting data with parity so lost pieces can be rebuilt). Clients reach it through signed URLs.
Delete blocks no version references, found by reference counts or mark-and-sweep, after a grace period so an in-flight commit cannot lose a block it just deduped against.
A per-device position in the change log. 'Changes after cursor N' is safe to repeat and survives lost notifications.
Commit carries its base version; if head moved on, reject and keep both copies instead of last-writer-wins.

lab.prompt: Design a Dropbox-like file sync service for 100 million registered users, about 20 million active per day, averaging 20 file changes per day each. Sketch the client, the services, the two stores, and the data model, then explain what happens when two devices edit the same file offline.
requirements: Edits to large files upload only changed data, not the whole file
A new version becomes visible to other devices only when all of its blocks are durably stored
Other devices learn of changes within a few seconds when online and catch up after being offline
Never silently lose a user's edit, even in a conflict
Handle roughly 400 million file changes per day, about 4,600 commits per second on average and several times that at peak
hints: Divide daily commits by 86,400 seconds, then multiply by a peak factor of 3 or more
Decide what the metadata row for a file version holds: version number, base version, ordered hash list
Think about what the per-user change log and its cursor look like, and what shards it
Let clients upload to the block store with signed URLs so the API tier stays light
Ask what a client must send with a commit so the server can detect a stale base

Blocks are shared. Decide how you know one is unreferenced (reference counts or mark-and-sweep), and wait a grace period before deleting so an in-flight commit cannot lose a block it just deduped against
Consider the privacy risk of cross-user dedup and what you would do about it
checklist: Client chunking and hashing step with a stated block size
Hash-existence check that returns only the missing blocks
Separate metadata store and block store with reasons
Per-user change log with a cursor for delta sync
Notification path treated as a hint, with a polling fallback
Base-version conflict check and a keep-both resolution
Block garbage collection plan for blocks no version references
